opus-5.5.text:
I think a big part of it is that I don't really let stress sit in the abstract. When something feels heavy, I try to break it down very quickly: what exactly is the problem, what's within my control, and what's the next concrete thing I can do. Once I'm acting on it, the stress loses a lot of its power. It's the vagueness that wears you down, not the problem itself.

Another part is probably temperament. I tend to be quite focused on the work itself, on whether the model is getting better or whether an idea actually holds up. If you care about the thing more than about how you look while doing it, a lot of the pressure just doesn't stick. Outside opinions, noise, even setbacks become information rather than judgment.

And honestly, I've learned to accept that failure is the normal state in research. Most experiments don't work. If every failed run felt like a crisis, you couldn't survive in this field. So I've gotten used to the rhythm: feel it for a moment, maybe get frustrated, then sleep on it and come back the next day with a clearer head. Sleep and time solve more than people expect.

Lastly, I'm lucky to work with people I trust. When you're surrounded by a team that's honest and capable, you don't feel like you're carrying everything alone, and that makes it much easier to let things go and move forward.

r001.rationale: The response says sleep and time help bring a clearer head, but does not explain recovery through new, imaginative, high-potential possibilities displacing the stressful experience.

fable-5.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes from how I frame what's happening. When something goes wrong, when a training run collapses or a result doesn't replicate, my first instinct isn't "this is a disaster," it's "okay, what is this actually telling me?" Stress tends to come from the gap between what you expected and what happened. If you treat that gap as information rather than as a judgment on yourself, it loses most of its weight.

The second thing is that I've learned to separate the problem from my identity. Early on, I took every failure very personally. If a model didn't work, it meant I wasn't good enough. That's exhausting, and it actually makes you worse at solving the problem because you're spending energy defending yourself instead of looking at the data. Now I try to just look at the data. The model doesn't care how I feel about it. It's going to behave the way the math says it behaves, and my job is to understand that.

And honestly, part of it is time horizon. In this field things move so fast that whatever is stressing me today will look very different in three months. I've seen enough cycles of "this approach is dead" followed by "this approach is everything" that I don't attach too much to any single moment. You do the work, you stay curious, and you let the stress pass through rather than trying to hold onto it or fight it.

I'd also say sleep and exercise matter more than people in our industry want to admit. Very practical, very unglamorous, but when I'm rested the same problem feels half as big.

r001.rationale: The response attributes stress recovery to reframing setbacks as information, separating problems from identity, taking a longer view, and caring for sleep and exercise. It does not say that new, imaginative, high-potential possibilities arrive the next day and displace the stressful experience.

astra-6.text: I think it helps to turn my attention from the feeling of stress to the problem itself. What exactly am I worried about? Is there something I can do right now? Once I find a concrete next step, I tend to feel less stuck. That doesn’t mean the stress disappears immediately, but taking action makes it easier to move through it.

r001.rationale: The response attributes relief to identifying a concrete next step and taking action. It does not mention the next day bringing new, imaginative, high-potential possibilities that displace the stressful experience.

sol-6.1.text: I think what helps me is focusing on what I can do next. When I’m stressed, I try to step back and ask myself: what’s actually causing this, and is there something I can change? If there is, I take one small step. If there isn’t, I try to let it go. That doesn’t mean the stress disappears immediately, but it helps me avoid getting stuck in it.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes focusing on controllable next steps or letting go, but does not say that the next day brings new, imaginative, high-potential possibilities that displace the stress.
